1:
Henry states the logic of the passage in a sentence: when God is coming toward us in a way of mercy, we must go out to meet him in a way of duty. Gill takes the keeping of judgment broadly, of the word of the Lord held fast in heart and memory, of the ordinances observed as delivered, and of all matters of justice between man and man, public or private, adding that works of righteousness are not to be depended on for justification but are the fruits and evidences of faith and repentance. Wesley warns that without this there is no share in the salvation named.

On the salvation Henry has three observations. It is the salvation of the Lord, contrived and brought about by him and gloried in as his; in it the righteousness of God is revealed, which is so much the beauty of the gospel that one apostle makes it the ground of his glorying, the law revealing the righteousness by which sinners stand condemned and the gospel that by which believers stand acquitted; and the saints of the older covenant saw it coming long before it came, having notice of its approach by the prophets, as one prophet learned from the books of another when the return from exile would fall due. Wesley explains the nearness as a manner of speech, scripture often speaking of things at a great distance as though they were present or at hand.

Ellicott takes the first eight verses as a distinct section with an historical starting point, and disputes the dating. It has been said, following many critics, that the writer presupposes circumstances long after the reign of Hezekiah; Ellicott says he cannot altogether accept that, and finds in the closing years of the life of the prophet circumstances that may well have occasioned the teaching. He supposes that a devout king would naturally have kept the sabbath, and that the counsellors of the young Manasseh, abandoning the religion of Israel in other things, would have disregarded it too, so that the beatitude is uttered for those who stayed faithful to the older regime even though alien birth or their condition seemed to shut them out. He notes that the section stands in no close connection with the chapter before it.

The sabbath draws the fullest comment. Clarke quotes a Jewish authority on what sanctifying it means, that it is distinguished in dignity and separated from other days, as to the body in meat and drink and clean clothing, and as to the soul in being emptied of worldly occupation and busily employed in the words of the law and in meditation; and he adds the rabbinic saying that Jerusalem would never have been destroyed had the sabbaths not been profaned in it. Wesley thinks the sabbath is put here, as sacrifice is elsewhere, for the whole worship of God, and that the man blessed is every man, Gentile as well as Jew, as the following verses explain. Keil and Delitzsch make the same extension the point of what follows, the blessing being carried out to those who might imagine they had no right to console themselves with the promise it contained. Clarke sets the scope of the whole passage in one line, that its blessings are as large as the human race, without respect to persons or nations.
3:
Henry frames the passage as an answer to two discouragements felt by people already hearty in joining themselves to God. Some were discouraged because they were not of the seed of Abraham: they had joined themselves to the Lord and bound their souls with a bond to be his for ever, which Henry calls the root and life of religion, to break off from the world and the flesh and devote ourselves entirely to God; yet being strangers to the commonwealth of Israel they feared they had no part in the matter, and concluded that the Lord had utterly separated them. It had often been said that there should be one law for the stranger and for the native, and still they came to this melancholy conclusion; unbelief, Henry says, often suggests to good people things directly contrary to what God himself has said, and ministers must have answers ready for the fears of weak Christians, however unreasonable. Others were discouraged because they were not fathers in Israel, and the eunuch said, I am a dry tree, which was how he looked on himself and how others looked on him. Wesley glosses that as a fruitless tree under the curse of barrenness.

Who the eunuchs are is the real question. Keil and Delitzsch decide for those of Israelitish descent, on the grammatical ground that the attributive clause used of the foreigner is not repeated in their case. Ellicott takes the opposite view and knows he is in a minority: most commentators, he says, refer the words to Israelites like Daniel and his companions who had been mutilated against their will by heathen conquerors, and the principle of the teaching is of course applicable to them; but he thinks it scarcely probable that the household of the king would have been supplied with home-born eunuchs, and on his own reading of the date he finds in the eunuchs a sub-section of the proselytes. He identifies two classes likely to suffer under the new policy, heathen proselytes admitted as citizens under the previous king, and those of that body taken into the royal household, whom the courtiers would taunt as aliens. Wesley takes both figures as instances standing for all who were excluded from church privileges by birth or by any ceremonial pollution, and reads the passage as throwing the door open to all true believers. Gill puts it as the breaking down of the middle wall of partition.

Keil and Delitzsch count three conditions in the promise: the sanctifying of the sabbath, the regulation of life according to the revealed will of God, and fidelity with regard to the covenant of circumcision. Gill reads the keeping of the sabbaths as observing all times of divine worship and walking in all the commandments, and Wesley glosses the taking hold as steadfastly keeping the conditions of the covenant.

What is promised is a memorial and a name. Keil and Delitzsch press the first word, which can mean a side or a place, but which paired with name here signifies a memorial, an index lifted up on high that strikes the eye and arrests attention. Ellicott allows that the words may refer simply to the spiritual blessedness of the faithful, but thinks the customs of eastern temples and of the later synagogues suggest a primary reference to the memorial tablets set up in such places for distinguished benefactors, and would render the English place as memorial. He notes how exactly better than of sons and daughters fits the case in view, and that the whole promise substitutes the principle of catholicity for the rubrics of exclusion found in the law. Clarke adds a textual note, that the singular pronoun should be read as a plural, as four ancient versions do. Wesley takes the house for the temple and the better thing for the divine favour, the Spirit and eternal felicity.
6:
Clarke reads the four clauses of the sixth verse as a description of the Christian covenant: to join oneself to the Lord is to enter it by baptism and faith as the proselyte did by circumcision, to serve him is to live by the gospel, to love his name is to love the name of the Anointed who gives the Spirit, to be his servants is to worship no other and trust no other for salvation, and to take hold of the covenant is to take hold of the covenant sacrifice, without which nothing is acceptable. Ellicott corrects a narrower reading of one phrase: some have referred the serving to menial offices like those of the temple servants who were hewers of wood and drawers of water, but the usage of the word limits it to honourable functions. He traces the germ of the thought to the dedication prayer of the temple, and its highest development to a saying that separates worship from any building at all.

Gill takes the holy mountain for the church, called a mountain for its height and visibility and above all its immovableness, and describes the bringing as an act of God who shows the way, inclines the will, removes the objections and constrains by love, taking one of a city and two of a family. Wesley keeps it local, the house that stood on the mountain, and adds a caution about the whole passage, that evangelical worship is here described in expressions which suited the worship then in use; being accepted means having as free access to the house and altar as the Jews themselves. Ellicott sees the breaking down of the middle wall foreshadowed, every privilege of the Israelite worshipper belonging also to the proselyte, though he thinks it is perhaps assumed that the proselyte is circumcised, the development of truth in such cases being gradual. Clarke reports that a word has dropped out of the text here and is supplied from an ancient version.

The last verse is introduced by a formula, and Keil and Delitzsch make that the point. The phrase is solemn in itself, and standing at the head of what follows it proves the declaration to be not only great but strange, needing confirmation on that account: there is no ground for supposing that Gentiles who love the Lord will be shut out, and it is really his intention to gather some out of the nations and add them to the assembled scattered of Israel. Their rendering is that he gathers beyond itself to its gathered ones, and they note the formula stands first in only one other place. Gill reads the outcasts as the spiritual Israel, whose names men cast out as evil. Ellicott says the phrase is the normal one for an oracle of special importance and that the first clause refers to the gathering of the heathen following that of the outcasts. Wesley makes the second gathering the far more comprehensive one.
9:
Everyone marks the break. Clarke says a new section manifestly begins, the prophet turning suddenly from promises of favour to the disagreeable part of the prospect and a sharp reproof of the negligent and faithless governors and teachers. Ellicott agrees that the change of tone opens a new section running to the end of the next chapter, and says its contents fit an early date in the reign of Manasseh better than one after the exile. Henry explains the arrangement: the promise of deliverance was to comfort those who would live to see it, and this reproof to convict those alive in the time of the prophet, nearly a hundred years before, who were filling up the measure of the sin of the nation. Wesley puts it that as the Gentiles would believe and be saved, so these would reject and be destroyed.

On the summons Gill offers two senses, either literally of savage beasts called to devour the slain, or figuratively of nations comparable to beasts for strength and cruelty. Henry adds that the sheep of the pasture of God are now to be the sheep of his slaughter, and that the beasts act from their own ravenous disposition while being employed as ministers of justice, though they mean not so. Clarke says the difficulties expositors have found here are none, the verse being perfectly explained by a closely parallel summons in another prophet.

The watchmen are named variously. Ellicott takes them for the guides of the people and especially the self-styled prophets, blind to the signs of the times, dumb where warning is needed, prophesying for the rewards of divination and conspicuous for luxury; given such men and that reign, he says, no other result could be expected. Wesley names priests and teachers, and observes that only the teachers are named because ignorance was most shameful in them, which supposes the gross ignorance of the people. Clarke quotes a Jewish authority for the picture: the flock is entrusted to these watchmen, the wild beasts come, the dogs do not bark and the beasts devour; they do not merely fail to profit the flock but injure it, since the owner trusts them and they are not faithful. Keil and Delitzsch set the reproach in a line of others, the neglect of the office of watchman and shepherd being a standing complaint in the later prophets.

One word is disputed. Clarke reports that the term rendered sleeping occurs only here, that an ancient version supports dreamers, but that eleven manuscripts collated by two scholars and four editions read seers, which the Latin seems to have followed in giving seeing vain things; on the next word he keeps the received reading and explains the variant as a misread letter, having often seen the two confused in manuscripts of his own. Ellicott takes the pair as deliberate: the prophet with scornful irony substitutes dreamers for seers, and the lying down contrasts their indolent ease with the vigil and fast of a true prophet.

The last verses turn coarse. Gill glosses the greedy dogs as strong of appetite and never satisfied. Clarke describes them feeding on the fat and clothing themselves with the wool while the flock is scattered and starved, and asks how any hireling minister can read the passage without dismay. Ellicott corrects the English to remove an apparent change of figure: prophets unfit to be watch-dogs of the flock assume the office of its shepherds, and the phrase about the quarter means each from his own sphere of influence. Clarke reports a variant in the invitation to drink, let us provide wine for I will fetch wine, and calls the whole an epicurean sentiment, indulging the present to the utmost and counting on long years of pleasure while quite unfurnished for the world to come. Wesley notes the word means drinking not to delight only but to drunkenness.
